sweep_summary: One stress-titled item for Gooniyandi: Crowhurst (1995, WCCFL 13). for the session was exhausted (2000/2000) and Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex could not be reached by automated download/no-budget, so the copy was located through the Rutgers Optimality Archive index spreadsheet (ROA.xlsx): it is ROA-19, an open pre-print of the WCCFL 13 paper, now saved and read in full (17 PDF pages, text). It is a secondary OT analysis resting wholly on McGregor 1990:120-125: initial stress on every di-/polysyllabic morpheme, iterative left-to-right binary trochees within the prosodic word, never final stress, with footnote 2 openly setting aside the vowel-length complications of tri-/quinquesyllabic morphemes -- so it CONFIRMS the catalog's weight-hedged coding and adds nothing first-hand; nothing left to acquire (priority none). Best first-hand statement actually read in this search of works with stress in the title is McGregor's 1984 Sydney thesis (already held by the project), sec. 2.5.1 pp.103-104, giving the mora-based S1/S2 stress rules verbatim; it corroborates but does not supersede the catalog's deciding source (McGregor 1990, the published revision of the same section). Kager 1992, the catalog's corroborating secondary, was not re-examined (not a works with stress in the title). Data note: the on-disk from 9/16 contains a generic unfiltered Glottolog page (Z-alphabetical entries, 460382 total records), not the Gooniyandi reference list; a refetch today returned HTTP 406, so this search of works with stress in the title relied on the target file's Glottolog 5.1 item list.

new_statements.quote: To account for these patterns, I distinguish the mora from the syllable. A syllable consists of one or more morae: open syllables of the form CV (V short) have a single mora, and closed syllables of the form CVC, or syllables with a long vowel (i.e. of the form Caa) have two morae. Stress may be assigned to morae sequences as follows: 2 morae SU / 3 morae SUU / 4 morae SUSU / 5 morae SUUSU ... S1 A syllable is stressable if one if its morae is stressed. S2 If two successive syllables are stressable, only one may receive stress, and it is usually the syllable with the most morae.

new_statements.reading: First-hand describer's statement: stress is predictable and delimitative (p.100: 'No two roots are distinguished by placement of stress, which is predictable'); default is initial stress with alternation (disyllables SU, trisyllables usually SUU, four syllables S-U-S-U with primary 'usually going onto the third syllable', five SUUSU), but stress is assigned over MORAE, so closed syllables and long-vowel syllables (2 morae) attract stress: trisyllables with a closed final get SUS (final 'usually bears primary stress, although sometimes the initial syllable has equal or stronger stress', p.102), and trisyllables with a heavy second syllable get USU (pil'kaali, ma'ntaarra, ka'rajpi). This is exactly the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding (initial/alternating default, weight-sensitive under S1/S2, author hedging on primary placement); it confirms it in full running text, wording near-identical to the 1990 grammar's pp.119-120 passage quoted in the catalog.

The weakness was evidential form, not source choice: snippets only, grade 'snippet'. The author's 1984 Sydney thesis, downloaded now (open access, text), gives the same section in full running text (pp.100-104) with the same patterns, mora definitions and S1/S2 rules, so the reading is confirmed in context and the strength of the evidence can be raised from 'snippet' (cite the thesis pages as full-text corroboration alongside the 1990 locators). sources.quote: Diyari (Austin 1981, Poser 1989), Dyirbal (Dixon 1972), and Gooniyandi (McGregor 1990), languages of Australia, are metrically similar in assigning stress initially in all morphemes containing at least two syllables. In Diyari and Gooniyandi, the third syllable of a quadrisyllabic morpheme is also stressed. [fn. 2:] Stress in Gooniyandi is complicated by vowel length in trisyllabic and quinquesyllabic morphemes. However, within morphemes containing an even number of syllables, regardless of vowel length, and in most trisyllabic morphemes, the facts are as described here.
